claim: The Golgi complex plays a central role in protein processing, sorting and transport.

claim: In higher eukaryotes the Golgi complex consists of multiple stacks of polarized flattened cisternae.

claim: Cisternae polarization allows for the directional transport and sequential processing of newly synthesized proteins arriving at the cis-face of the Golgi complex from the endoplasmic reticulum.

claim: At the trans-Golgi network (TGN), fully processed proteins are sorted and exported to other compartments of the secretory pathway or for secretion.

claim: Despite the large influx and efflux of membrane-bound transport carriers, the overall morphology of the Golgi complex remains essentially unaltered.

claim: Golgi cisternae are characterized by having a relatively large area-to-volume ratio to accommodate the large numbers of incoming and outgoing transport carriers and also to efficiently regulate the enzymatic reactions occurring at the Golgi membranes.
source: Golgi cisternae are characterized by having a relatively large area-to-volume ratio to accommodate the large numbers of incoming and outgoing transport carriers and also to efficiently regulate the enzymatic reactions occurring at the Golgi membranes (Klumperman, 2011).

claim: A Golgi cisterna consists of two geometrically distinct regions with very different membrane curvatures: the central cisterna part, which is almost flat with the seldom presence of fenestrations or pores; and the highly bent rim of the cisterna.
source: Moreover, a Golgi cisterna consists of two geometrically distinct regions with very different membrane curvatures: the central cisterna part, which is almost flat with the seldom presence of fenestrations or pores; and the highly bent rim of the cisterna.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Golgi structure

claim: Disruption of sphingomyelin (SM) organization specifically at the Golgi membranes by SM synthase-mediated formation of short-chain SM at the trans-Golgi membranes leads to inhibition of transport carrier formation.
source: We previously reported that disruption of sphingomyelin (SM) organization specifically at the Golgi membranes –by SM synthase-mediated formation of short-chain SM at the trans-Golgi membranes– leads to inhibition of transport carrier formation (Duran et al., 2012)

claim: Disruption of sphingomyelin (SM) organization specifically at the Golgi membranes leads to defects in transmembrane protein glycosylation and localization.
source: We previously reported that disruption of sphingomyelin (SM) organization specifically at the Golgi membranes –by SM synthase-mediated formation of short-chain SM at the trans-Golgi membranes– leads to inhibition of transport carrier formation (Duran et al., 2012) and also to defects in transmembrane protein glycosylation and localization (van Galen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Galen et al., 2014, which is the authors' previous work

claim: Short-chain SM might not be able to generate liquid-ordered nanodomains at the Golgi membranes.

claim: A flat cisterna has a large surface area at its rim with a very high membrane curvature thereby bearing large elastic stresses.

claim: Cisterna curling is accompanied by a change in the distribution of the membrane elastic stresses.
source: Hence, cisterna curling is accompanied by a change in the distribution of the membrane elastic stresses.

source: The shape of cellular organelles, such as the Golgi complex, results from the generation and stabilization of the curvature of their membranes (Shibata et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shibata et al., 2009

claim: According to the elastic model of membrane bending, energy is required to induce local changes of the membrane curvature from its preferred or spontaneous curvature.
source: According to the elastic model of membrane bending (Helfrich, 1973; Campelo et al., 2014), energy is required to induce local changes of the membrane curvature from its preferred or spontaneous curvature.
evidence: Supported by citations to Helfrich, 1973 and Campelo et al., 2014

claim: The amount of bending energy associated with local curvature deviations is proportional to the local bending rigidity of the membrane.
source: This energy is generally supplied by specialized lipids and/or membrane proteins, usually referred to as membrane curvature generators (Zimmerberg and Kozlov, 2006; McMahon and Gallop, 2005; Kozlov et al., 2014). Moreover, the amount of bending energy associated with local curvature deviations is proportional to the local bending rigidity of the membrane (Helfrich, 1973).

claim: Both local variations in the amounts of curvature generators present on the membrane and in the bending rigidity of the membrane can influence the morphology of Golgi cisternae.

claim: Experimental evidence has suggested the existence of nanoscopic SM-enriched liquid-ordered domains at the Golgi membranes.

claim: Direct visualization of nanoscopic SM-enriched liquid-ordered domains at the Golgi membranes has remained challenging.

evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Liquid-ordered membrane domains are expected to have a higher bending rigidity than the surrounding liquid-disordered membrane.

evidence: Supported by citations to Roux et al., 2005; Heinrich et al., 2010; Dimova, 2014

claim: Liquid-ordered membrane domains are less prone to accommodate membrane curvature than liquid-disordered membrane.

claim: The presence of large amounts of rigid nanodomains at the highly curved rim of a flat Golgi cisterna is associated with a large bending energy penalty.
source: In essence, the presence of large amounts of such rigid nanodomains at the highly curved rim of a flat Golgi cisterna is associated with a large bending energy penalty.

claim: Inhomogeneous curvature-driven nanodomain redistribution is entropically unfavorable.

claim: The flat-to-curled morphological transition is associated with a reduction of the bending energy of the rim, but also with an increase in the bending energy of the central region of the cisternae.

claim: Budding events are more frequent at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, where the membrane is already curved thus facilitating this process.

claim: A reduction in the amounts of membrane curvature generators present at the cisterna rim leads to an increase of the bending energy penalty of the rim, which could in turn be relaxed by a flat-to-curled shape transition.

claim: The time scale of mechanical equilibration of the cisterna shape is much smaller than that of the changes in lipid and protein composition through membrane fluxes.

claim: The equilibrium configuration of a cisterna is assumed to correspond to a free energy minimum.

claim: A partial release of membrane curvature generators destabilizes the flat shape in favor of a curled cisterna shape.

claim: For lower values of the spontaneous curvatures (0≤Js < 0.016 nm−1), the only stable shape is that of a curled Golgi cisterna.

claim: Nanodomain partitioning from rim to sheet is enhanced upon a reduction in the spontaneous curvature of the Golgi cisterna.

source: Besides the reduction in the levels of long-chain SM and the concomitant increase in short-chain SM levels, this treatment also causes an increase in the amounts of diacylglycerol (DAG) at the Golgi membranes by 30% (from 1.4 to 1.8 mol%) (Duran et al., 2012).

claim: The fast flip-flop rate of DAG allows DAG molecules to homogeneously redistribute between the two membrane monolayers unless an active mechanism imposing DAG inter-monolayer asymmetry exists.

claim: The increase in the levels of DAG is not the driving force for the observed curling of the Golgi cisternae.

claim: The metabolic generation of SM at the Golgi membranes results, via a DAG-triggered signaling pathway, in the local reduction of PI(4)P levels causing the release of PI(4)P-binding proteins, such as the clathrin-adaptor protein γ-adaptin, without affecting the localization of COPI components.
source: It has been recently found that the metabolic generation of SM at the Golgi membranes results, via a DAG-triggered signaling pathway, in the local reduction of PI(4)P levels causing the release of PI(4)P-binding proteins, such as the clathrin-adaptor protein γ-adaptin, without affecting the localization of COPI components (Capasso et al., 2017).

claim: After 30 min of treatment with short-chain ceramide, the pool of clathrin-HC initially present at the Golgi membranes was mostly released.

claim: The formation of curled cisternae upon the treatment with short-chain ceramide proceeds in parallel with a decrease in the amounts of curvature inducers at the Golgi membranes.

claim: After 4 hr of D-cer-C6 treatment, virtually no flat stacks are observed.

claim: Cisternae curling occurs towards the trans-Golgi cisternae/TGN.

claim: The measured radii of flat and curled cisternae are in agreement with the condition of area conservation.

claim: A 2 hr short-chain ceramide washout is sufficient to recover similar levels of clathrin-HC at the Golgi membranes as to those found in untreated cells after a 30 min pre-treatment.

claim: Recovery of normal clathrin-HC levels at the Golgi membranes after a 4 hr D-cer-C6 treatment occurs in about 6 hr.

claim: Even 16 hr after the short-chain ceramide washout, both flat and curled Golgi cisternae can still be observed.

claim: The curling of the Golgi cisternae induced by short-chain ceramide is accompanied by a lateral segregation of different Golgi-resident proteins, such as TGN46 and p230.

claim: After short-chain ceramide washout, the recovery of the levels of clathrin-HC at the Golgi membranes occurs much faster than the recovery of the flat cisternae morphology and of protein colocalization.

claim: The experimental results are indicative of a hysteretic behavior of the transition from flat-to-curled cisternae and reverse, as the model predicts.
